concepts.name: Reading a sector's percentage
concepts.description: Each sector's label or legend gives its share of the whole pie directly.

concepts.name: Angle and percentage
concepts.description: A full circle is 360°, so every percentage point equals 3.6°.

concepts.name: Converting a share into an amount
concepts.description: Multiply a sector's percentage by the total to get its actual quantity.

concepts.name: Comparing sectors
concepts.description: Differences and ratios between two sectors, in either percentage or actual quantity.

concepts.name: Finding the total from one sector
concepts.description: If you know one sector's actual amount and its percentage, you can work backwards to the whole total.

formulas.title: Angle from percentage
formulas.prompt: How do you convert a sector's percentage into its central angle?
formulas.explanation: This works in reverse too: divide an angle by 3.6 to recover its percentage.
formulas.example: 25% of a pie has a central angle of 25 × 3.6 = 90°
formulas.commonMistake: Multiplying by 3.6 only for some sectors and not others, or confusing it with 360.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A sector represents 25% of the data. What is its central angle?

formulas.title: Value from a percentage share
formulas.prompt: How do you find the actual quantity a sector represents?
formulas.explanation: The percentage tells you the fraction of the total; multiplying by the total converts that fraction into a real quantity.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting to convert the percentage to a decimal (or fraction) before multiplying.

formulas.title: Finding the total from one sector
formulas.prompt: If you know one sector's actual value and its percentage, how do you find the total?
formulas.explanation: This is the value formula rearranged — dividing by the percentage (as a decimal) undoes the multiplication.
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing by the percentage number itself (15) instead of the decimal (0.15).
formulas.applicationPrompt: ₹6,000 represents 15% of a budget. What is the total budget?

formulas.title: Degrees and percentages at a glance
formulas.prompt: Which pie-chart angles should you recognise as percentages instantly?
formulas.explanation: The whole pie is 360° = 100%, so divide degrees by 3.6.
formulas.example: A 54° sector is 15% of the total.
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing by 360 and forgetting to multiply by 100.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A sector is 126°. What percentage is it?

formulas.title: Compare sectors without the total
formulas.prompt: How do you compare two sectors when the total is not given?
formulas.formula: Value ratio = angle ratio (or percentage ratio)
formulas.explanation: Every sector is the same fraction of the same total, so the total cancels.
formulas.example: Sectors of 72° and 108°: their values are in the ratio 2 : 3.
formulas.commonMistake: Working out each value from a total that is not needed.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Rent is 30% and food 45% of a budget. If rent is ₹12,000, what is food?

levels.title: Shares of a Whole
levels.description: Every sector represents a percentage of the total — the whole pie is always 100%.

blocks.title: Percent, angle, or amount
blocks.body: A pie chart can label its sectors by percentage, by angle, or leave you to compute an actual amount from the total. All three describe the same underlying share — you just need to convert between them.
When comparing two sectors, their percentages are already proportional to each other — you don't need to convert to actual amounts unless the question asks for rupees.

levels.title: Pie Charts Formulas
levels.description: Percentages, angles, converting to actual values, and working backwards to the total.

levels.title: Direct Reading
levels.description: Reading percentages, angles, and simple values.

levels.title: Comparing and Scaling
levels.description: Comparing sectors, and scaling the whole budget up.

levels.title: Working Backwards
levels.description: Finding the total from one sector, and multi-step adjustments.

questions.question: What percentage of the budget is spent on Food?
questions.context: Study the pie chart of a monthly household budget and answer the question.

chart.caption: Monthly household budget of ₹40,000, by category
chart.ariaSummary: Monthly household budget: Rent 30%, Food 20%, Transport 10%, Savings 25%, Other 15%, of a total of ₹40,000.

questions.method: Read the percentage directly from the sector or legend.

hints.text: This is a direct reading, no calculation needed.

questions.question: What is the central angle of the sector representing Savings?

chart.caption: Monthly household budget of ₹40,000, by category
chart.ariaSummary: Monthly household budget: Rent 30%, Food 20%, Transport 10%, Savings 25%, Other 15%, of a total of ₹40,000.

questions.explanation: Savings is 25% of the pie. Angle = 25 × 3.6 = 90°.

questions.question: How much is spent on Transport (in ₹)?

chart.caption: Monthly household budget of ₹40,000, by category
chart.ariaSummary: Monthly household budget: Rent 30%, Food 20%, Transport 10%, Savings 25%, Other 15%, of a total of ₹40,000.

questions.method: Convert the percentage to a decimal, then multiply by the total.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert the percentage to a decimal first.

questions.question: How much more is spent on Rent than on Other (in ₹)?

chart.caption: Monthly household budget of ₹40,000, by category
chart.ariaSummary: Monthly household budget: Rent 30%, Food 20%, Transport 10%, Savings 25%, Other 15%, of a total of ₹40,000.

questions.method: Convert both sectors to actual amounts before subtracting.

hints.text: Do not subtract the percentages and call it the answer in rupees.

commonMistakes: Subtracting the percentages (30−15=15) and treating that as a rupee amount.

questions.question: What is the ratio of the amount spent on Savings to the amount spent on Transport?

chart.caption: Monthly household budget of ₹40,000, by category
chart.ariaSummary: Monthly household budget: Rent 30%, Food 20%, Transport 10%, Savings 25%, Other 15%, of a total of ₹40,000.

questions.explanation: Savings = 25%, Transport = 10%. Since both are percentages of the same total, their ratio equals 25:10 = 5:2.
questions.method: Percentages of the same total can be compared directly as a ratio.

hints.text: You do not need to convert to rupees first — the percentages are already proportional.

commonMistakes: Converting to rupees unnecessarily and making an arithmetic slip.

questions.question: If the total budget increases to ₹50,000 with the same percentages, how much would be spent on Rent (in ₹)?

chart.caption: Monthly household budget of ₹40,000, by category
chart.ariaSummary: Monthly household budget: Rent 30%, Food 20%, Transport 10%, Savings 25%, Other 15%, of a total of ₹40,000.

questions.method: The percentage stays fixed; only the total changes.

hints.text: Use the new total, but the same percentage.

commonMistakes: Using the old total of 40,000 by mistake.

questions.question: What is the combined percentage spent on Food and Transport together?

chart.caption: Monthly household budget of ₹40,000, by category
chart.ariaSummary: Monthly household budget: Rent 30%, Food 20%, Transport 10%, Savings 25%, Other 15%, of a total of ₹40,000.

questions.method: Percentages of the same whole simply add.
commonMistakes: Averaging the two percentages instead of adding them.

questions.question: The amount spent on Other is ₹6,000. Using only this and the pie chart's percentages, what is the total monthly budget (in ₹)?

chart.caption: Monthly household budget of ₹40,000, by category
chart.ariaSummary: Monthly household budget: Rent 30%, Food 20%, Transport 10%, Savings 25%, Other 15%, of a total of ₹40,000.

questions.explanation: Other is 15% of the total. Total = 6,000 ÷ 0.15 = 40,000.
questions.method: Divide the known amount by its percentage, as a decimal.

hints.text: This reverses the usual percentage-to-value calculation.

questions.question: If ₹2,000 is moved from Savings to Food, what would be the new percentage spent on Food?

chart.caption: Monthly household budget of ₹40,000, by category
chart.ariaSummary: Monthly household budget: Rent 30%, Food 20%, Transport 10%, Savings 25%, Other 15%, of a total of ₹40,000.

questions.method: Convert to actual amounts, adjust, then convert back to a percentage.

hints.text: Work in rupees first, then convert the new amount back to a percentage.

commonMistakes: Simply adding percentage points without converting to actual amounts.

questions.question: Which stream's sector has a central angle of 54°?
questions.context: Study the pie chart of a college's students by stream and answer the question.

chart.caption: Students of a college by stream (total 2,400 students)
chart.ariaSummary: Students by stream: Engineering 35%, Commerce 20%, Science 18%, Arts 15%, Law 12%, of a total of 2,400 students.

questions.explanation: Each 1% of the pie is 3.6°, so 54° ÷ 3.6 = 15%. Arts is the 15% sector.
questions.method: Convert the angle back to a percentage, then find that sector in the legend.

hints.text: Convert the angle back to a percentage by dividing it by 3.6.

questions.question: The number of Commerce students is approximately what percentage of the number of Engineering students?

chart.caption: Students of a college by stream (total 2,400 students)
chart.ariaSummary: Students by stream: Engineering 35%, Commerce 20%, Science 18%, Arts 15%, Law 12%, of a total of 2,400 students.

questions.explanation: Both sectors are shares of the same total, so compare the percentages directly: 20 ÷ 35 × 100 ≈ 57.1%, so the nearest option is 57%. (In students: 480 ÷ 840 gives the same.)
questions.method: Shares of the same total compare exactly like the actual numbers.

hints.text: You do not need the actual numbers — the sector percentages are already in proportion.

commonMistakes: Answering the gap of 15 percentage points.

questions.question: By what percentage is the number of Science students more than the number of Law students?

chart.caption: Students of a college by stream (total 2,400 students)
chart.ariaSummary: Students by stream: Engineering 35%, Commerce 20%, Science 18%, Arts 15%, Law 12%, of a total of 2,400 students.

questions.explanation: Science = 18% and Law = 12% of the same total. Science exceeds Law by (18 − 12) ÷ 12 × 100 = 50%. In students: 432 and 288, and 144 ÷ 288 × 100 = 50% too.
solutionSteps: Science 18%, Law 12%: a gap of 6 percentage points.
Divide the gap by Law's share: 6 ÷ 12 × 100 = 50%.
questions.method: Percentage more = gap ÷ the share being compared against × 100.

hints.text: The 6-point gap is not the answer — divide it by Law's share.
"More than Law" makes Law the base.

commonMistakes: Answering 6%, the gap in percentage points.
Dividing by Science's 18% instead of Law's 12% (≈ 33.3%).

questions.question: Next year the college's total rises to 3,000 students and Commerce's share rises to 24%. By what percentage does the number of Commerce students increase?

chart.caption: Students of a college by stream (total 2,400 students)
chart.ariaSummary: Students by stream: Engineering 35%, Commerce 20%, Science 18%, Arts 15%, Law 12%, of a total of 2,400 students.

questions.method: Convert both years to actual numbers before comparing, because the totals differ.

hints.text: Turn both years' shares into actual numbers of students first.
The totals differ, so the shares 20% and 24% cannot be compared directly.

commonMistakes: Answering 4% (the change in percentage points) or 20% (24 vs 20), both of which ignore the larger total.
